1.pericope_label: Our entrance was not vain: Philippi, and the disclaimers of deceit, uncleanness and guile

schools.summary: Correct the rendering so that the coming was not vain rather than not in vain, and distinguish the word for hollow from the word for fruitless; explain that the shame at Philippi lay in treatment undeserved and unlawful, and that the indignity to a Roman citizen still rankled, Acts and the epistle throwing light on each other; weigh whether the first disclaimer means deceit or error, and what argument each would commit the apostle to; and divide over uncleanness, whether it points at the consecrated impurities of pagan religion or at the subtler temptations of spiritual work itself.

Take the word of empty show rather than of fruitless result, as of an ambitious man who makes a display and has nothing solid; and sort the three disclaimers by department, the first touching the substance of the doctrine, the second the affections of the heart, the third the manner of acting.

Press the word for conflict as meaning not merely earnest labour but peril of life; find the uncleanness disclaimed among the Gentile philosophers and the gods celebrated for their crimes; observe that the word for exhortation carries consolation, so that such preaching is comfort throughout; and note that the term for uncleanness is not always confined to lust.

Report both readings of the disputed phrase without choosing between them, and observe that it is a great comfort to a minister when his own conscience and the consciences of others witness together that he set out well.

debates: Whether the entrance is called not vain as to its result or as to its character.
What the shame of the treatment at Philippi consisted in, and why Paul names it.
Whether the first disclaimer denies deceit or denies error, and what follows from each.
Whether the uncleanness disclaimed belongs to pagan religion or to the temptations of ministry.
outliers: Barnes alone draws from the passage a rule that an abused man need not smooth the matter over.
Robertson alone reports that the indignity to a Roman citizen still rankled years afterwards.
Ellicott alone tests a proposed reading by asking what argument it would commit the apostle to.
Ellicott alone turns the charge of uncleanness inward upon the temptations of spiritual work.
Calvin alone distributes the three disclaimers across doctrine, motive and method.

4.pericope_label: Approved of God to be entrusted: neither flattery, nor covetousness, nor glory of men

schools.summary: Show that the word rendered allowed means examined and approved, and that the tense argues from habitual practice; call the claim a confident profession of loyalty that should be every preacher's ambition; distinguish the witnesses, since flattery could be judged by men but covetous design by God alone; explain the word for cloak as a show put forward to hide an intent; prefer the marginal sense of dealing heavily in apostolic pomp over the sense of financial burden; and extend the title of apostle to the companions named.

Guard the claim of approval against any boast of native fitness, since Paul does not set his own power against the grace of God; define flattery doctrinally, as preaching the purity of human nature and the power of free will instead of original sin and man's impotency; argue that whoever aims to please men must stoop to flattery while whoever aims at duty will avoid its appearance; and deny that the last clause refers to money, since the apostle waived his claim to authority itself.

Notice that the appeal is to men for what men could see and to God for what only God could see, and to both where the matter is mixed; and settle the disputed word by the Hebrew term answering to it, which signifies weight and glory alike — then turn from the text to ask the clergy whether they can call God to witness that their ministry has no end but his glory, or whether they entered the priesthood for what is impiously called a living.

debates: What the word rendered allowed implies, and whether it leaves room for any native fitness.
What flattery consists in — a manner of address, or a doctrine of human ability.
Why Paul appeals to men for one charge and to God for another.
Whether the burden he might have imposed is financial support or the weight of apostolic authority.
outliers: Gill alone makes the refusal to flatter a matter of doctrine, listing what such preaching must deny about human nature.
Wesley and Ellicott independently observe that the choice of witness follows what a witness could know.
Clarke alone leaves the exposition to arraign the clergy of his own communion over the word living.
Calvin alone rules out the financial sense of the last clause on the ground that the apostle waived authority itself.
Ellicott alone suggests the episcopal office may here be ranked with the apostolate.

7.pericope_label: Gentle as a nurse, imparting our own souls, and labouring night and day

schools.summary: Prefer the reading babes on the manuscript evidence against four scholars who prefer gentle for the sense; press the possessive in the figure, since it is the mother-nurse who suckles her own; set the apostles against the fawning and greedy teachers the Greeks were used to; grade the love that tells a sinner the way of salvation above the love that warns a man in danger; trace the rare verb of longing to a sepulchral inscription; and separate the two words for toil as kind and intensity.

Reject the reading babes as impossible on the sense, since the Thessalonians are the children and the apostle the nurse, and no man can be both at once; infer from the wording that the stay at Thessalonica was much longer than is supposed, with the days given to manual work and the evenings to preaching; and figure the apostle as a hen surrounded by her young.

Report the variant and decline to choose between the readings, since either yields the same voluntary abasement; describe the nurse's affection as rare and wonderful, sparing no labour and cheerfully giving her own blood to be sucked; and argue that since the churches are bound to maintain their ministers, the apostle in laying no burden on them did more than his office required, and was moved by some special consideration.

Observe that this gentleness came from one entitled to use an apostle's authority, and that such behaviour is the way to win people rather than to rule with rigour, as a nursing mother bears with frowardness and stoops to mean offices for a child's good.

Lay down that a teacher must do nothing with a feeling of burden which tends to his disciples' salvation, since if Jacob was buffeted night and day keeping flocks, much more must the man entrusted with souls endure toil however mean — and set the apostle's manual labour against the ordinance that those who preach should live of the gospel.

debates: Whether the text says the apostles were gentle among them or became babes among them.
What the figure of the nurse is meant to establish, and against whom it is drawn.
How imparting one's own soul differs from imparting the gospel.
How the days and nights at Thessalonica were divided between labour and preaching.
outliers: Robertson alone follows the manuscripts to the harder reading and defends it against the scholars who prefer the easier one.
Clarke alone refutes that reading by the impossibility of a man being both the child and the nurse.
Calvin alone declines the textual question on the ground that the doctrine is unaffected either way.
Ellicott alone quotes a contemporary Frenchman for the maxim that a minister should keep a mother's heart.
Clarke and Barnes divide the working day in opposite ways, one preaching by night and the other by day.

10.pericope_label: Holily, justly and unblameably: dealing with every one as a father, that they might walk worthy of God

schools.summary: Justify the appeal to God from the maxim that righteousness lies in the mind with which an act is done; mark the limits of the claim, which is to consistency and faithfulness rather than absolute perfection; infer from the passage a stay longer than the three sabbaths recorded in Acts; find in the words about every one a glimpse of the apostolic method of dealing with individual souls; and restore the tense of the calling, altered by scribes to avoid a difficulty, since the call is a continual beckoning and not a momentary act.

Make the third adverb a matter of reputation and explain that the servants of Christ cannot escape calumny from a world that hates them, so the claim is restricted to those who judge uprightly; require of a pastor that he be a father to his church, adding particular instruction to public teaching; and define lively preaching as that which does not merely tell men what is right but summons them to the judgment-seat of God, asking what must be done with us if men so prompt needed stirring.

Distribute the three adverbs among God, men and ourselves; marvel that no hypocrite could appeal at once to God and to his hearers; compress the three participles into willingly, joyfully and carefully; and divide the kingdom from the glory as the church here and heaven hereafter, while allowing the phrase may be a hendiadys for a glorious kingdom.

debates: Why God as well as the hearers is called to witness.
How the three adverbs are to be distributed, and what the added words about believers qualify.
What the passage shows about the apostolic method and the length of the stay.
Whether the calling is a past act or a continuing one, and whether kingdom and glory are two things or one.
outliers: Ellicott alone supports the appeal to God by a maxim of Aristotle.
Calvin and Ellicott explain the clause about believers in opposite ways, one restricting the jury to fair judges and the other naming the likeliest place of temptation.
Barnes alone states what the claim does not amount to, denying that absolute perfection is asserted.
Ellicott alone argues that the tense of the calling was altered by scribes to remove a theological difficulty.
Calvin alone turns the commendation of the Thessalonians into a reproach of his own readers.

13.pericope_label: Received not as the word of men: imitators of the Judean churches, and the invective against the persecutors

schools.summary: Distinguish the two verbs for receiving, an outward reception and a welcome; make the ground of conviction decisive for endurance, since faith won by reasoning or eloquence or deference will not survive a fiery trial; read the likeness to the Judean churches as a likeness in suffering, and as evidence against the theory of a feud between Paul and the Twelve; qualify the charge that they do not please God; and note that the writer had himself been such a persecutor, doing what he now condemns in the belief that he pleased God.

Turn the imitation of the Judean churches against the claims of Rome, which the apostle would have named as the model had it possessed any preeminence; draw a numbered indictment of the persecutors and press it to its limit; and narrow the charge of enmity to all men, resting it chiefly on the effort to keep others from hearing the gospel.

Argue that once the word is taken for God's, obedience follows of necessity, so that the contempt many show for scripture reveals what they take it to be; grant that the apostle strips the persecutors of all honour, but read the charge corporately, of a body whose resistance to God was nothing new rather than of the same individuals; and name the difficulty underneath, that converts harried by the one nation which gloried in God's name might doubt the religion they had embraced.

Draw three consequences from the manner of receiving — that the gospel comes by men of like passions with ourselves, that it is nevertheless God's word in truth, and that those are greatly to blame who give out their own fancies for it.

debates: What difference the two words for receiving mark, and why the ground of conviction matters.
In what respect the Thessalonians imitated the churches of Judea, and what follows from the comparison.
Whether the charge against the persecutors is laid on individuals or on a body, and how far it extends.
How converts should understand being persecuted by those who claim to be the people of God.
outliers: Barnes alone argues that faith resting on reasoning, eloquence or deference will not survive persecution.
Clarke alone turns the choice of the Judean churches as model into an argument against the primacy of Rome.
Robertson alone cites the passage as evidence against the theory of a feud between Paul and the Twelve.
Robertson and Ellicott alone recall that the writer had himself persecuted the church in the belief that he pleased God.
Ellicott alone uses the invective to defend the authorship of the fourth Gospel against a standing objection.

16.pericope_label: Filling up their sins, the wrath come upon them, and the bereaved apostle hindered by Satan

schools.summary: State the charge precisely, that the objection was not to speaking with Gentiles but to their being saved otherwise than as Jews; read the filling up of sin as the tendency of the conduct rather than its intention, and extend the principle to a church or a person; correct the conjunction and the tense of the coming wrath; press the word for bereaved as describing an orphan, tracking the succession of figures from nurse to babe to father to orphan; and take the singular pronoun as an undesigned agreement with the movements recorded in Acts.

Explain that the length of the polemic answers a calumny which divided churches and took from the Gentiles the hope of salvation, so that the passage removes a stumbling-block; note that even believing Jews at first disapproved the mission to the nations; and hold that when the wicked molest us they fight under Satan's banner as his instruments, wishing all pious minds were impressed with how continually he contrives to obstruct the church.

Complain that a word meaning bereft of children is tamely translated; identify the hinderer with the persecuting Jews, or allow either the devil or one of his children, and add that his friends thought it imprudent to let him go till the storm abated; and distinguish the transient affections that flow like a torrent in the apostle from the abiding tenderness and fixed posture of soul from which they flow.

Turn the phrase about an hour on the reader: our time on earth is short and uncertain whether we are with our friends or apart from them, and this world is not a place where we are long to be together, since it is in heaven that holy souls meet and never part.

debates: What exactly the persecutors forbade, and whether the objection was to Gentiles hearing or to Gentiles being saved as Gentiles.
Whether filling up the measure of sin describes an intention, a tendency, or a divine permission.
What the word rendered taken from you conveys, and how it fits the figures used earlier.
Whether the hinderer is Satan himself, his human instruments, or circumstances.
outliers: Barnes alone narrows the charge by distinguishing what the Jews did and did not hold unlawful.
Calvin alone explains the length of the invective as answering a calumny that was costing the Gentiles their hope.
Ellicott alone extends the principle about a completed measure of sin from a nation to a church and a single person.
Robertson alone counts the four figures the apostle passes through in one chapter.
Wesley alone distinguishes the apostle's torrential passions from the settled temper underneath them.

19.pericope_label: Our hope, our joy, our crown of rejoicing at his coming

schools.summary: Distinguish what the words do not mean, since the converts are neither the foundation of hope nor the thing hoped for nor its ground, but persons hoped well of; guard the crown against any glorying save in God, while allowing that we may glory in his favours in their own place; and conclude that ministers will share glory on the last day according as each has promoted the kingdom, and should learn now to rejoice in nothing but the issue of their labours.

Divide over the image, some taking the crown for the garland of a victor at the games and one proposing instead the chaplet given to an arriving king, the word for the coming being almost technical in the papyri for a royal arrival; read the passage as an answer to the insinuation that the apostle did not really wish to return; and close by denying both that a minister's acceptability proves him unfaithful and that the offence he gives proves him faithful.

Put the argument as a question, why a man who has forsaken everything and has no prospects from earth should labour at the risk of his life except to save souls; turn the chapter into an examination for preachers, most of whom on reading it honestly will either resign or resolve to work harder, since those who enter for applause or emolument have their reward without one smile from Christ; and close by asking that the Christian world treat the Jews with humanity and mercy.

debates: In what sense converts can be called a minister's hope without displacing Christ.
Whether the crown is an athlete's garland or the chaplet given to an arriving king.
How a minister should read the acceptability or the offensiveness of his own preaching.
What is owed to those the chapter has just denounced.
outliers: Gill alone lists three things the converts are not, before saying what they are.
Robertson alone proposes the royal arrival rather than the games as the source of the figure, and supports it from the papyri.
Robertson alone reads the passage as a reply to an insinuation that the apostle did not wish to return.
Barnes alone rules out both inferences at once, that being pleasing proves unfaithfulness and that giving offence proves fidelity.
Clarke, who drew up a six-count indictment of the persecutors four verses earlier, closes the chapter by asking that the Jews be treated with humanity and mercy.
